The difference between true and reported gaze position, typically reported as error in degrees of visual angle; larger error indicates poorer accuracy (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.367).
The reproducibility of a gaze position from sample to sample under a stable true gaze, typically reported as RMS-S2S or STD (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.367).
The amount/proportion of eye-tracking data lost, counterpart to tracking ratio or availability (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.368).

Duration from an actual eye movement to the corresponding gaze sample being output by the eye tracker; also known as end-to-end delay or temporal accuracy (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.368, citing Reingold 2014, p.641).
The process of mapping eye-tracker measurements to physical gaze direction or position, via fitting procedures, biologically plausible models, or a combination (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.367).
A segment of stimulus space identifying a portion of the stimulus meaningful to the experimental design, enabling dwell-time, hit-rate, and transition calculations (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.368).
The number of gaze direction/position measurements made per second (Hz), ranging from ~10Hz in web-camera trackers to 10000Hz in some recordings (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.367).

The segmentation of an eye-tracker signal into meaningful events (fixation, saccade, smooth pursuit, etc.) with start, end, and duration; terminology varies across the field (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.368, citing Hessels et al. 2018).

target: Salvucci, D. D., & Goldberg, J. H. (2000)
note: Originators of the I-DT (dispersion-threshold) and I-VT (velocity-threshold) fixation/saccade detection algorithms, foundational to nearly all subsequent event-detection software (FE, ~p.391).
NH2010 noise-adaptive event-detection algorithm, an improvement on I-VT that adapts the peak-velocity threshold to data noise level and outputs detected post-saccadic oscillations (FE, ~p.391).
I2MC algorithm, designed to be robust against increasing levels of noise and data loss common in infant eye-tracking research (FE, ~p.391).

GazeNet, a fully end-to-end machine-learning event detector that learns from examples and detects fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations with very high resemblance to human expert coders (FE, ~p.391).

Four-measure framework (RMS-S2S, STD, BCEA, power-spectrum-slope 'noise colour') for fully characterizing precision in gaze data, cited throughout the paper's data-quality sections (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.369, 389).

The authors' own eye-tracking methodology textbook, the single most frequently cited background reference throughout the paper (chapters on eye-tracking methods, setup/geometry, event detection, AOI analysis) (FE, throughout).
Meta-study of 33 experiments concluding eye-movement measures of cognitive load are more sensitive than heart-rate, skin, and brain (EEG) measures (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., ~p.383).

Found precision significantly poorer in SMI Vive VR goggles compared to SMI glasses, though accuracy differed only in some conditions (mostly when fixation-point distance changed) (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.377).
Found the end-to-end latency of common VR headsets ranged from 45-81ms (FAITHFUL-Holmqvist et al., p.377).
Foundational demonstration that pupil dilation tracks memory-task load, cited as the origin of the mental-workload/arousal-pupil-dilation literature this paper reviews (FE, ~p.383).
